title: WAYS TO SELL EXISTING PHYSICAL PRODUCTS
content:
If you would rather sell physical products that already exist, the biggest difference between your options is how involved you want to be in the transaction.

With wholesale or resale, you generally acquire products and resell them to your customers. With dropshipping, you make the sale but a supplier fulfills the order. With affiliate or referral marketing, you send the customer to another merchant and earn according to that merchant's program.

Those differences affect inventory, cash requirements, margin, fulfillment, returns, control, and the customer relationship.

WHOLESALE / RESALE
You generally acquire inventory before the customer buys it. That gives you more control over stock and fulfillment but ties money up in inventory.

DROPSHIPPING
You make the sale while another business stores and ships the product. Inventory requirements can fall while supplier dependence rises.

AFFILIATE / REFERRAL
You usually send the customer to another merchant and receive compensation for a qualifying attributed transaction.

THE QUESTION TO ASK
How much of the retail transaction do you actually want to own? More control usually creates more responsibility. Less responsibility usually means giving up some control and economics too.

QUICK COMPARISON
Wholesale/resale: More inventory responsibility, more control over the retail transaction.
Dropshipping: Less inventory handling, strong supplier dependence, you still operate the sale.
Affiliate/referral: Least control over the transaction, merchant handles the sale, compensation depends on attribution.

If none of those roles appeal to you because you want control over the product itself, return to PDF 12.

I WANT TO BUY AND RESELL PRODUCTS → PDF 17.
I WANT TO SELL WITHOUT HOLDING THE INVENTORY MYSELF → PDF 18.
I WANT TO REFER THE CUSTOMER TO THE MERCHANT FOR COMMISSION → PDF 19.
I THINK I WANT MY OWN PRODUCT AFTER ALL → PDF 12.

WHAT CHANGES BETWEEN THESE MODELS
All three routes can put an existing physical product in front of a customer, but they place responsibility in different places.

Wholesale/resale moves inventory risk toward you.
Dropshipping moves fulfillment toward the supplier while leaving you responsible for the customer sale.
Affiliate/referral moves the retail transaction toward the merchant and makes your income dependent on qualifying attribution.

That is why the same physical product can support three very different businesses.

WHO CONTROLS WHAT?

Wholesale or resale usually means you buy products and then resell them. That gives you more direct control over what inventory you have available and often more control over the customer experience, but it also means money can be tied up in stock that has not sold.

Dropshipping removes the need to hold the item yourself before a customer orders. The supplier ships it after the sale. That can reduce inventory exposure, but it also means the supplier's stock accuracy, packaging, shipping speed, and product consistency become part of an experience your customer may associate with you.

Affiliate or referral selling moves even more of the transaction to the merchant. You recommend or refer the customer, but the merchant usually handles checkout, fulfillment, returns, and the ongoing customer account. Your compensation then depends on the program's attribution and commission rules.

A product you love can still be a poor fit for the role you want to play. Use this guide to choose the relationship you want with the product and transaction before you spend time looking for specific suppliers or programs.

FOLLOW ONE PRODUCT THROUGH THREE MODELS

Suppose the product is a desk lamp that retails for $60.

WHOLESALE / RESALE
You buy 20 lamps from a supplier for $30 each, spending $600 before you have customers. You now have 20 units to sell. When a customer buys one from you for $60, the retail transaction is yours. Depending on how you operate, you may store it, pack it, ship it, handle the customer's questions, and deal with returns. If only five lamps sell, the remaining 15 are still your inventory.

The advantage of having stock available and controlling more of the transaction exists because you accepted the inventory commitment.

DROPSHIPPING
You list the lamp without buying 20 units first. A customer pays you $60. You then place or transmit the order to the supplier, who charges its price and ships the lamp to the customer.

You avoided purchasing a batch in advance, which is why inventory risk can be lower. But you also did not personally control whether the supplier actually has the lamp, how quickly it leaves the warehouse, how it is packed, or whether the item matches expectations. Your customer can still hold your store responsible for the experience.

AFFILIATE / REFERRAL
You recommend the lamp and send the customer to the merchant. The merchant collects the $60, fulfills the order, and handles the transaction. If the purchase meets the affiliate program's attribution rules, the merchant pays you the stated commission.

This removes even more day-to-day responsibility because you are no longer the retailer. It also removes control. You normally cannot decide the merchant's price, checkout, inventory, return policy, or whether the affiliate program changes later.

The three models can involve the exact same physical lamp. What changes is your role in the transaction.

1. WHO PAYS FOR INVENTORY BEFORE THE CUSTOMER BUYS?
With wholesale/resale, that may be you. With dropshipping or affiliate marketing, you may avoid purchasing a batch first.

2. WHO TAKES THE CUSTOMER'S PAYMENT?
A reseller or dropship store usually does. An affiliate normally sends the customer to the merchant.

3. WHO IS RESPONSIBLE FOR GETTING THE ITEM TO THE CUSTOMER?
A reseller may fulfill it directly or hire fulfillment. A dropship supplier ships it for your store. In affiliate marketing, the merchant handles the retail order.

4. WHAT DO YOU CONTROL?
Generally, more retail responsibility gives you more control over the transaction and more things to manage.

5. WHAT ARE YOU DEPENDENT ON?
Every route has dependencies: suppliers, inventory, marketplaces, merchants, affiliate terms, shipping carriers, or fulfillment partners.

The best route for you is not automatically the one with the fewest tasks. It is the one whose combination of control, commitment, workload, and dependence you prefer.

WHAT HAPPENS WHEN SALES GROW?

The models create different scaling problems.

With wholesale/resale, stronger sales usually mean you need more inventory. That can require more cash before the next batch sells, more storage, more packing or fulfillment capacity, and better inventory planning.

With dropshipping, you may not need to finance the same inventory yourself, but order volume increases your exposure to the supplier's capacity and reliability. Ten late shipments are ten customer problems even if you never touched the boxes.

With affiliate marketing, a large increase in referrals may create very little additional fulfillment work for you because the merchant handles the transaction. Your business can still become more dependent on the merchant, platform, traffic source, and affiliate program that make those commissions possible.

So "scalable" does not simply mean "can make more money." Ask what resource becomes strained when sales increase: cash, inventory, labor, supplier capacity, customer support, or dependence on an outside program.

WHAT TO VERIFY IN A REAL OPPORTUNITY

For wholesale, verify actual product cost, minimum orders, shipping, payment terms, authorized sales channels, return arrangements, and relevant brand restrictions.

For dropshipping, verify supplier pricing, stock reliability, shipping times, tracking, returns, damaged-order handling, product quality, and what happens when inventory information is wrong.

For affiliate marketing, verify current commission terms, attribution rules, prohibited promotion methods, payment thresholds or schedules, return or reversal treatment, and program-change provisions.

Those facts turn the conceptual comparison in this guide into a real business decision.

IF YOU ARE STUCK BETWEEN RESELLING, DROPSHIPPING, AND AFFILIATE

Use responsibility as the tiebreaker.

WHOLESALE/RESELLING gives you the strongest version of being the retailer in this comparison, including inventory responsibility.

DROPSHIPPING lets you remain the customer retailer while outsourcing physical fulfillment to a supplier.

AFFILIATE MARKETING moves the retail transaction to the merchant. You create the referral rather than operating the store transaction.

If your instinct is, "I want the customer to buy from ME," compare wholesale and dropshipping.

If your instinct is, "I mainly want to recommend the right products without becoming the store," compare affiliate marketing.

That one distinction should make the next PDF easier to choose.

THE DECISION

If you want to be the retailer, compare wholesale/resale with dropshipping based largely on whether you want to hold inventory yourself. If you mainly want to create the recommendation and let another merchant own the transaction, affiliate marketing is the cleaner branch.

WHERE TO GO NEXT
Choose PDF 17 for wholesale/resale, PDF 18 for dropshipping, or PDF 19 for affiliate/referral. Return to PDF 12 if what you really want is control over the product itself.
